He was known for careful scholarship and many hours spent copying manuscripts, some of which still survive. Even more, he was known for charity. He lived simply, slept little, and gave away nearly everything to the poor. Students in Kraków remembered his warmth and fairness. He died in 1473 and was canonized in 1767. John shows that study and holiness belong together when knowledge leads to love.

saints.name: Saint Stephen
saints.subtitle: Deacon and martyr · Jerusalem, c. 35
saints.summary: One of the first deacons and the first Christian martyr, who died forgiving those who stoned him.
saints.bio:
Saint Stephen appears in the Acts of the Apostles as one of seven men chosen by the apostles to serve the Church in Jerusalem, especially the widows who needed food. Acts describes him as full of faith and of the Holy Spirit, and as a man who worked wonders among the people.

His preaching stirred opposition, and he was brought before the Jewish council. He answered with a long speech recalling the history of Israel and declaring that Jesus was the Righteous One. His hearers dragged him outside the city and stoned him. Like Jesus on the cross, he prayed for his killers. A young man named Saul watched and approved; he would later become the apostle Paul. Stephen’s feast, the day after Christmas, reminds us that the Child of Bethlehem calls for a faith ready to forgive.
saints.quote: Lord Jesus, receive my spirit.

saints.name: Saint John
saints.subtitle: Apostle and evangelist · first century
saints.summary: The apostle and evangelist whom tradition identifies as the beloved disciple, who stood at the cross and received Mary as his mother.
saints.bio:
Saint John was a fisherman of Galilee, the son of Zebedee and the brother of Saint James. Jesus called the two brothers from their nets and named them “sons of thunder.” With Peter and James, John witnessed the Transfiguration and the agony in the garden.

The Church has long identified him with the disciple whom Jesus loved, who rested on his breast at the Last Supper, stood at the foot of the cross, and was given Mary as his mother. Tradition credits him with the fourth Gospel, three letters, and the Book of Revelation, and holds that he died in old age at Ephesus. His writings return again and again to one theme: God is love. His symbol is the eagle, for the soaring vision of his Gospel. John invites us to rest close to the heart of Jesus.
saints.quote: God is charity: and he that abideth in charity abideth in God, and God in him.

saints.name: The Holy Innocents
saints.subtitle: Child martyrs · Bethlehem
saints.summary: The Church honors the baby boys of Bethlehem killed by King Herod in his attempt to destroy the newborn Christ.
saints.bio:
The Gospel of Matthew tells that after the Magi came seeking the newborn king of the Jews, King Herod grew afraid of a rival. When the wise men did not return to him, he ordered the killing of all the boys in and around Bethlehem who were two years old and under. Joseph, warned in a dream, had already fled to Egypt with Mary and the Child.

Matthew saw in this grief the fulfillment of Jeremiah’s words about Rachel weeping for her children. Bethlehem was a small town, and the number of children killed is not known. The Church has honored them as martyrs since early centuries, because they died in place of Christ. Coming in the days after Christmas, this feast reminds us to defend the lives of the smallest and most vulnerable.
saints.quote: A voice in Rama was heard, lamentation and great mourning; Rachel bewailing her children, and would not be comforted, because they are not.

saints.name: Saint Thomas Becket
saints.subtitle: Archbishop and martyr · c. 1120–1170
saints.summary: The archbishop of Canterbury who defended the freedom of the Church against King Henry II and was murdered in his own cathedral.
saints.bio:
Saint Thomas Becket was born in London around 1120. Able and ambitious, he became chancellor of England and a close friend of King Henry II. In 1162 Henry made him archbishop of Canterbury, expecting a loyal ally. Instead Thomas changed. He took up prayer and penance and began to defend the rights of the Church against the king’s attempts to control it.

The quarrel drove Thomas into exile in France for six years. Soon after he returned, four knights, angered by the king’s furious words, entered Canterbury Cathedral on December 29, 1170, and killed him. All of Europe was shocked. Thomas was canonized in 1173, and the king did public penance at his tomb. Canterbury became one of the great pilgrim shrines. Thomas shows that conscience owes its first loyalty to God.

saints.name: Saint Sylvester I
saints.subtitle: Pope · died 335
saints.summary: The pope who led the Church of Rome as persecution ended under Constantine and the first great public churches were built.
saints.bio:
Saint Sylvester became bishop of Rome in 314, just after Emperor Constantine ended the persecution of Christians. After centuries of hiding and martyrdom, the Church could now worship openly, and during his long reign great churches rose in Rome, including the Lateran Basilica and the first Saint Peter’s.

The Council of Nicaea met in 325 during his time as pope. He did not attend himself but sent representatives. Many later legends grew up around him, including stories that he baptized Constantine and received a grant of power from him; these are not historical. He died in 335 and was among the first saints honored in Rome who were not martyrs. Because his feast falls on December 31, New Year’s Eve is called Silvester in parts of Europe. Sylvester reminds us that peace, too, is a time for faithful work.
